title: Given a scenario, configure Microsoft Windows networking features on a client/desktop

subtopics.heading: Workgroup vs domain
subtopics.notes:
Workgroup
- Each device is standalone
- Each device keeps its own usernames and passwords
- Sharing across devices means duplicating credentials
- Typical for home networks

Windows domain (Active Directory)
- One central database of users, devices, printers, permissions
- One set of credentials per user, used across every domain-joined device
- IT admins manage everything from one place
- Requires a domain controller (separate server). Not used at home
- Windows Home cannot join a domain; needs Pro or higher

Joining a domain:
- Settings > System > About > Domain or Workgroup > Change
- Or Control Panel > System > Change settings
- Need domain admin credentials with rights to add a computer to the domain
subtopics.whyOnExam: If the scenario mentions central IT, single sign-on, or thousands of devices, the answer involves a domain (Active Directory). Home environments stay on workgroups.
subtopics.commonTrap: Trying to domain-join a Windows Home machine. The option is grayed out / unavailable - Home cannot join AD.

subtopics.heading: Shared resources and mapped drives
subtopics.notes:
A Windows share = a file, folder, or printer made available on the network.

Hidden / administrative shares
- Append a $ to the share name to hide it from the browse list
- ADMIN$, C$, IPC$ are built-in administrative shares
- 'Hidden' only means it won't show in pull-down lists. Anyone who knows the path can still connect

View local shares: Computer Management > Shared Folders

Map a network drive:
- File Explorer > Three dots > Map network drive
- Pick a drive letter, enter \\server\share, optionally reconnect at sign-in, optionally use different credentials
- Or run net use H: \\server\share at the command line
- For share names with spaces, quote the path: net use H: "\\server\Gate Room"

Disconnect: three dots or right-click in File Explorer.
subtopics.whyOnExam: $ at the end means hidden share. UNC path format is \\server\share. net use H: \\server\share is the CLI map command.
subtopics.commonTrap: Assuming hidden shares are secured by hiding. They're not - users who know the path can still connect. Use permissions for actual security.

subtopics.heading: Windows Defender Firewall
subtopics.notes:
Built-in stateful firewall, on by default.

Separate rule sets per profile:
- Private network
- Public network (most restrictive)
- Domain network (when joined to AD)

Basic config (Control Panel > Windows Defender Firewall): turn on/off per profile, block all incoming (even allowed rules), notify on blocked apps.

Advanced rules (Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security):
- Inbound rules - what is allowed IN
- Outbound rules - what is allowed OUT
- Connection security rules - IPsec
- Monitoring - live status

New rule wizard (right-click > New Rule):
1. Rule type: Program, Port, Predefined, Custom
2. Protocol + port (e.g. TCP 80)
3. Local + remote IP scope
4. Action: Allow / Allow if secure / Block
5. Profiles to apply to (Domain / Private / Public)
6. Name + description

Example: 'Block unencrypted web traffic' = inbound rule, TCP, local port 80, action Block.
subtopics.whyOnExam: Know the rule-creation steps and that the profile is automatic based on the network you're connected to. Block-by-port is the right answer when no specific app needs to be blocked.
subtopics.commonTrap: Disabling the firewall to fix a connectivity issue. Add an inbound rule for the specific port or app instead.

subtopics.heading: Client IP configuration
subtopics.notes:
DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol)
- Default for almost all client OSes. Server hands out IP, mask, gateway, DNS
- Lease has a duration; client renews periodically

APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing)
- Fallback when DHCP is unavailable AND no static address is set
- Range: 169.254.1.0 through 169.254.254.255
- Also called 'link-local' - LAN-only, no internet
- 169.254.x.x in ipconfig = DHCP failed

Static IP
- Manually configured on the client OR
- DHCP reservation tied to the device's MAC (manages from the server side, recommended)

Required settings for any IP config:
- IP address (unique on the subnet)
- Subnet mask (defines the subnet)
- Default gateway (router for off-subnet traffic)
- DNS server (resolves names to IPs)

Loopback address: 127.0.0.1 (any 127.x.x.x). Tests the local TCP/IP stack without leaving the device.

Alternate Configuration tab
- Lets a client try DHCP first, fall back to a specific manual config if DHCP fails (instead of APIPA)
- Useful for laptops that move between DHCP networks and a fixed lab
subtopics.whyOnExam: 169.254.x.x = DHCP failed. 127.0.0.1 = loopback. Memorize both ranges and what they mean diagnostically.
subtopics.commonTrap: Confusing APIPA (169.254.x.x) with link-local IPv6 (fe80::/10). Both are 'link-local' but the IPv4 range is the one tested by 220-1202.

subtopics.heading: Network connection types
subtopics.notes:
Wired Ethernet - cable into NIC. Fastest, always the default if multiple connections are active.

Wireless (Wi-Fi)
- SSID = wireless network name
- Security type: WPA2 / WPA3 (personal uses pre-shared key PSK, enterprise uses 802.1X with central auth)
- Encryption: TKIP (legacy WPA1) or AES (WPA2 / WPA3). WPA2 / WPA3 always use AES

VPN (Virtual Private Network)
- Client software on laptop encrypts traffic, sends through a public network
- VPN concentrator on the corporate side decrypts and forwards
- Set up via Network and Sharing Center > Set up a new connection > Connect to a workplace
- Often paired with MFA (smart card = something you have)

WWAN (Wireless Wide Area Network)
- Cellular: hardware adapter, USB modem, or smartphone tether / hotspot
- May require third-party software for the hardware
subtopics.whyOnExam: WPA2 / WPA3 = always AES. TKIP is the legacy WPA1 cipher and is the trap answer. Wired is the default route when multiple connections coexist.
subtopics.commonTrap: Picking TKIP for a modern WPA2 / WPA3 deployment. The exam consistently tests AES as the only correct cipher for WPA2 / WPA3.

subtopics.heading: Proxy, network profile, metered connection
subtopics.notes:
Proxy settings
- Sits between you and the internet, makes requests on your behalf
- Configure: Control Panel > Internet Options > Connections > LAN Settings, OR Settings > Network and Internet > Proxy
- Auto-discover, script URL, or manual server / port
- Exceptions list lets specific apps bypass the proxy

Network profile (per connection)
- Private: home / work, file sharing typically allowed
- Public: coffee shop / hotel, NO inbound, NO file sharing - safest default
- Domain: appears when joined to AD

When you connect to a new network, Windows asks if it is private or public; this choice maps to firewall + sharing behavior.

Metered connection
- Tell Windows the link costs money or has data caps
- Reduces background data: throttles Windows Update, OneDrive sync, app updates
- Set per connection: Settings > Network and Internet > [adapter] > Metered connection toggle
- Can set a data limit and reset cycle
subtopics.whyOnExam: If a scenario mentions cellular hotspot or a capped link, metered connection is the answer. Public profile is the safest answer for an untrusted Wi-Fi.
subtopics.commonTrap: Marking a coffee shop network as Private out of habit. Public is correct - Public disables file sharing and tightens inbound rules.
